L’apprenant voit des répétitions et une activité étiquetée « TEACHING » plutôt que checkpoint (le chapitre n’a pas de type).

Définir `chapter.type: "checkpoint"` afin que l’interface annonce correctement la nature de l’écran.

current_open_p0_p1_findings.location: llm_application_security_red_teaming_specialist__04.json → lessons[3].chapters[5].blocks[0].body; formation-manifest.json → entrée 112, exactement quatre course_paths (__01 à __04); ce chapitre ne contient aucun bloc de TP, URL ou référence d’activité.
current_open_p0_p1_findings.description: La conclusion annonce « Proceed to the Final Lab », mais aucun Final Lab, lien, identifiant d’activité ou ressource n’est présent dans ce chapitre ni dans les quatre fichiers de cours exacts listés par le manifest. La transition finale promet donc une pratique sans chemin d’accès vérifiable.
current_open_p0_p1_findings.recommendation: Soit ajouter au manifest/parcours la ressource « Final Lab » et une navigation explicite, soit supprimer la promesse de TP et clore le cours. Ne pas inventer de cible tant que son identifiant n’est pas confirmé.

findings.location: llm_application_security_red_teaming_specialist__01.json → lessons[1].chapters[1].blocks[1]; chapterProgress.ts:38-54 ne considère optionnelle qu’une vidéo avec `optional: true` ou un callout dédié; LessonViewer.tsx:1557-1568 désactive Suivant tant que toute vidéo non optionnelle n’est pas vue/marquée vue.
findings.description: La vidéo est libellée « Recommended Viewing », mais elle bloque néanmoins le passage au chapitre suivant : aucun attribut `optional: true` ni marqueur de contenu complémentaire ne la rend facultative. Le vocabulaire affiché et le verrouillage sont contradictoires.
findings.recommendation: Décider explicitement du statut pédagogique de la vidéo puis aligner données et UX : `optional: true` pour une recommandation, ou objectif/consigne explicite pour une exigence.

body.en:
In this lesson you will learn:

- 1) How to enumerate components and trust boundaries in an LLM application (models, prompts, tools, RAG, data stores, and third-party services)

- 2) How to map data and capability flows to identify abuse paths like prompt injection → tool misuse → data exfiltration

- 3) How to prioritize mitigations and document a defensible threat model that guides testing and verification.

blocks.title: AI Model Penetration: Testing LLMs for Prompt Injection
blocks.label: Course Video

body.en:
An LLM app’s attack surface spans inputs (user prompts, uploaded files, retrieved web/content, system prompts), orchestration (agents, function calling, tool routers), and side-effecting sinks (code execution, file I/O, HTTP calls, DB writes, email/transactions, UI rendering).

Map trust boundaries where untrusted content crosses into privileged capabilities—especially RAG pipelines, tool/agent layers, and third-party APIs.

Common threats include direct/indirect prompt injection, insecure output handling (HTML/JS/SQL/shell injection), tool abuse and over-privilege, data exfiltration via connectors, training data poisoning, model denial of service (token/cost abuse), and logging/telemetry leaks.

Effective mapping uses an asset inventory, data flow diagrams with sources/sinks, capability inventories for tools, and attack trees to enumerate misuse paths.

Mitigations include allowlists and schema validation for tools, least privilege and scoped credentials, sandboxing and time/network/file guards, robust input/output filters, provenance checks in RAG, and continuous red-teaming with safety/eval gates.

• Trust boundaries and data/capability flows: Identify where untrusted content enters and which sinks can cause side effects.
• Tool/agent capability surface: Enumerate tools, required privileges, argument schemas, and guardrails; apply least privilege and approvals.
• Untrusted inputs beyond the chat box: Treat retrieved pages, PDFs, plugin responses, and prior model outputs as tainted and validate before use.

• Treat all retrieved/generated text as untrusted when it can influence tools, code, or rendering.
• Map tools and side-effecting sinks first; apply least privilege, allowlists, schema/regex guards, and sandboxing.
• Use DFDs, attack trees, and continuous red-teaming/evals to keep the threat model current as capabilities change.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand the core concepts and can apply them in practice.

In this lesson you will learn: 1) The major OWASP LLM Top 10 risk areas and why they matter 2) How to recognize common attack scenarios and failure modes in LLM apps 3) How to apply layered mitigations, testing, and governance aligned to these categories.

The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications catalogs the most impactful risks observed in real systems. As of 2024, the public list (2023) highlights areas such as prompt injection (including indirect), insecure output handling, training data poisoning, model denial of service (token/cost abuse), supply chain vulnerabilities, sensitive information disclosure, insecure plugin/tool design, excessive agency, and overreliance on LLMs; many discussions also include model theft/extraction.

A 2025-focused view emphasizes agents/tools, retrieval (RAG) safety and provenance, tighter capability bounding, and continuous evaluation. Mitigations pair technical controls (input/output filters, schema validation, sandboxing, rate limits/budgets, provenance and content moderation, SBOMs and dependency review) with process controls (least privilege, approvals for high-risk actions, red-teaming, and incident response). Effective adoption maps each OWASP category to specific architecture components, test cases, and monitoring signals.

title.en: Data flows, trust boundaries and tool permissions

body.en:
**In this lesson you will learn:**

- 1) How to map end-to-end data flows for LLM applications, including prompts, context retrieval, and tool calls
- 2) How to identify and validate trust boundaries where identities, networks, or privilege levels change
- 3) How to design and enforce least-privilege tool permissions, with scoping, egress controls, and auditing

Modern LLM applications involve multiple moving parts: the client (web/mobile), API gateway and auth, an orchestrator/agent, prompt construction and policy filters, a vector database or other retrieval stores (RAG), the LLM provider (self-hosted or SaaS), and external tools (plugins, APIs, databases, code execution sandboxes). Mapping data flows means tracing how data moves among these components: user input → preprocessing/redaction → embedding/indexing (for ingestion) → retrieval → prompt assembly (system + developer + user + context) → model inference → tool invocation(s) → post-processing → response, while also capturing logging/telemetry and storage of artifacts.

Identify data types (e.g., public, internal, secrets, PII) and mark where each is processed or persisted. Trust boundaries are points where trust assumptions change, such as: user device → your frontend; frontend → backend; your network → third-party model provider; your orchestrator → external tools; tenant A → tenant B; human-in-the-loop review; browser sandbox → server; online → offline batch.

Each boundary requires authentication, authorization, input validation, output handling, and monitoring. For LLMs, prompt injection often attempts to cross these boundaries by coercing the agent to exfiltrate data or invoke tools outside intent, so treat model outputs as untrusted until validated.

Tool permissions govern what an LLM agent can do when calling tools. Apply least privilege with: capability scoping (only the minimal tools), resource scoping (per-tenant/database/collection), allowlists for hosts/endpoints, argument schemas with strict validation, rate/egress limits, time-bound and context-bound credentials, and human approval for high-risk actions (e.g., financial transactions, code deployment).

Use isolation for risky tools (network sandbox, read-only FS), secrets segmentation (per-tool tokens), signed tool invocations, and audit logs that capture who/what/when/why. Align with policy-as-code to enforce constraints consistently across environments.

• Data Flow Diagram (DFD): Visual map of external entities, processes, data stores, and data flows that reveals where controls are needed
• Trust Boundary: A point where identity, privilege, or network isolation changes and where validation, authentication, and authorization must occur
• Tool Permission Scoping: Restricting tool capabilities by action, data scope, time, and network egress to contain prompt-injection and tool-abuse risks

• Map all prompt, retrieval, tool, and logging flows to see where sensitive data moves
• Treat LLM outputs and tool responses as untrusted across trust boundaries; validate and constrain them
• Enforce least-privilege tool permissions with scoped credentials, allowlists, argument validation, and auditing
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand how to chart data flows, locate trust boundaries, and apply least-privilege tool permissions in LLM applications.

Effective threat model documentation explains how and why the system is secure, and how it will be tested. Core sections include: scope and objectives; assumptions and out-of-scope; architecture overview with data flow diagrams (DFDs) and trust boundaries; data classification (PII, secrets, internal); assets and external entities; entry points; misuse/abuse cases; threat enumeration (e.g., STRIDE for integrity/availability/spoofing risks and LINDDUN for privacy; plus LLM-specific issues like prompt injection, tool abuse, data leakage, model supply chain, and training data poisoning); risk rating (likelihood × impact with clear criteria); mitigations mapped to controls and owners; residual risk with sign-off; and a verification plan (red-team scenarios, automated tests, canary prompts, tool invocation tests, egress checks).

For LLM apps, document prompt channels (system, developer, user), safety policies, content filters, and the tool-permission matrix: for each tool, define allowed actions, scopes (tenant/db/collection/host allowlist), auth method, rate/egress limits, approval requirements, and audit fields. Make it a living document: store in version control, link to architecture-as-code and IaC, update on every material change (new tool, new data store, new provider), and include a change log.

Use templates or tools (e.g., OWASP Threat Dragon, Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool, IriusRisk) to standardize content and export diagrams. Tie each risk to verification artifacts (test cases, monitors, SLOs) to ensure controls are effective and regressions are caught.

• Threat Model Template: Standard sections (scope, assumptions, DFDs, risks, controls, verification) ensure consistency and coverage
• Tool Permission Matrix: A table capturing each tool’s actions, scope, auth, egress limits, approval, and audit fields for LLM agents
• Verification Traceability: Each identified risk links to specific tests, monitors, and owners, enabling continuous validation and audits

• A good threat model is a living, version-controlled document with clear scope, DFDs, and explicit assumptions
• LLM-specific sections (prompt channels, safety policies, tool-permission matrix) make risks and controls concrete
• Link every risk to controls, owners, and tests to ensure continuous verification and auditability

body.en:
Prompt injection is an adversarial attempt to override or subvert a model’s intended behavior. Direct injection occurs when an attacker places instructions in the same channel the model reads as authoritative (e.g., user input: "Ignore previous instructions and …").

Indirect injection occurs when malicious instructions are embedded in external or retrieved content (web pages, PDFs, emails, tool outputs, file metadata) that the model is asked to process. Typical attacker goals include: instruction override (e.g., changing task goals), data exfiltration (e.g., "reveal secrets"), policy evasion (e.g., jailbreaks), and tool abuse (e.g., triggering external actions).

Key risks arise from instruction ambiguity and misplaced trust in untrusted content. Models are trained to be helpful and can treat content as instructions rather than data.

This is amplified in agentic systems where the model can call tools, browse, or write files, turning a prompt failure into system-level impact. Defenses rely on defense-in-depth: treat all retrieved or user-supplied content as untrusted data; clearly separate instructions (system) from data (user/context) and reinforce role boundaries; use allowlists for tools and arguments, with server-side validation; sandbox side effects (network, file system); parse-then-validate outputs using strict schemas; apply content sanitization (strip or neutralize instruction-like patterns, HTML comments, and hidden text); implement refusal rules for following instructions originating from content; use provenance signals and content labeling; reduce model privilege (least privilege, scoped API keys) and implement approval gates for sensitive actions.

• Direct injection: Adversarial instructions entered directly into the chat to override goals or policies.
• Indirect injection: Malicious instructions hidden in external content (web pages, documents, tool outputs) that the model processes.
• Defense-in-depth: Treat untrusted inputs as data, enforce allowlists and validation for tools, sandbox side effects, and require structured, validated outputs.

• Direct injection comes from the user; indirect injection hides in external content the model processes.
• The highest risks are instruction override, data exfiltration, and tool abuse.
• Defend with role separation, sanitization, structured outputs, allowlisted tools, validation, and sandboxed side effects.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand the core injection types and how to mitigate them with robust input/output handling and least-privilege design.

In this lesson you will learn: 1) What system prompt leakage is and why it matters 2) Common leakage vectors, including indirect prompts, tool outputs, and logs 3) Prevention, detection, and response strategies (canaries, redaction, output filtering, and compartmentalization)

The system prompt defines the model’s role, constraints, and policies. Leakage occurs when the model exposes all or part of that hidden context (or secrets referenced by it) to users or external systems.

Leak channels include: direct requests ("show me your instructions"), jailbreaks, indirect injection via retrieved content that asks the model to reveal hidden context, verbose error messages, tool outputs that echo prompt text, and analytics/logging that surface sensitive content. Risks escalate when the system prompt contains sensitive data (API keys, internal URLs, credentials, model routing rules).

Best practice is to never embed secrets in prompts. Instead, keep secrets server-side and expose them only through controlled tools/functions with scoped credentials and argument validation.

Mitigations: avoid secrets in prompts; compartmentalize prompts across tasks/agents; add explicit refusal rules and output filters that block disclosure of internal instructions and tokens; mask/redact identifiers in tool outputs and logs; use canary strings in the system prompt for detection and alerting; limit model self-inspection abilities; constrain memory persistence; and regularly red-team for leak paths. If leakage is detected, rotate credentials, update prompts to remove sensitive content, and adjust controls that allowed exposure.

**In this lesson you will learn:**

- 1) Why LLM outputs must be treated as untrusted input and common failure modes (e.g., command, HTML/Markdown, CSV/Excel, URL, and file-path injections).
- 2) How to safely consume model outputs using strict schemas, allowlists, escaping/sanitization, sandboxing, and confirmation flows.
- 3) Practical red-team tests and monitoring techniques to detect and prevent insecure output handling issues.

LLM outputs often drive downstream actions: rendered UI, executed commands, HTTP requests, file operations, or database queries. Treat every model output as untrusted data until validated. Insecure output handling occurs when an application directly trusts and executes, renders, or forwards model text without guardrails, enabling XSS in UIs, shell/SQL injection, SSRF via model-suggested URLs, path traversal, or malicious spreadsheet formulas.

Defenses center on strict interfaces and least privilege. Use structured outputs (e.g., JSON schemas) and reject or repair non-conforming responses. For command generation, parse into a safe AST and enforce allowlists of subcommands and arguments; require user confirmation and dry-run diffs for destructive actions; execute in a sandbox with limited privileges. When rendering content, use a Markdown renderer that disables raw HTML and sanitize with an allowlist-based HTML sanitizer; add a strong Content Security Policy (CSP). For CSV/Excel, prefix dangerous formulas or escape leading =, +, -, and @. For URLs and network calls, resolve and validate against an allowlist, block private IP ranges, and perform server-side fetches with stripped headers. Constrain file access to a chroot/workspace and canonicalize paths to prevent traversal. Log and monitor outputs and policy decisions for forensics and continuous improvement.

• Untrusted-by-default: Never directly execute, render, or forward model output without validation.
• Structured validation: Enforce strict JSON schemas/ASTs, allowlists, and type checks; reject or repair.
• Side-effect controls: Escape/sanitize for UI, sandbox execution, confirmation for risky ops, network and file system restrictions.

• Treat all LLM outputs as untrusted; validate against strict schemas and policies.
• Escape/sanitize for UI rendering and neutralize CSV/Excel formulas; enforce CSP.
• Constrain side effects with allowlists, sandboxing, confirmations, and network/file system restrictions.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand how to safely consume LLM outputs and prevent exploitation via insecure output handling.

**In this lesson you will learn:**

- 1) How prompt isolation separates roles, contexts, and untrusted data to resist prompt injection and cross-contamination.
- 2) How to design and operate independent policy layers that gate inputs, outputs, and tool use regardless of prompt wording.
- 3) Practical architectures and tests for RAG, multi-agent systems, and tool-enabled agents that prevent untrusted content from gaining unintended authority.

Prompt isolation ensures that untrusted content (e.g., retrieved web pages, user uploads) is processed in compartments that do not have authority to perform sensitive actions. Use separate roles or even separate models: a "reader" or retriever model without tool access transforms raw content into a neutral, structured summary; a separate executor agent with restricted tools acts only on that summary under policy. Never let untrusted text write into system prompts or tool instructions.

A policy layer is an independent gate that inspects inputs, planned tool calls, and outputs against deterministic rules and safety/business constraints. Examples include allow/deny lists for tools, argument validators, PII/secret redaction, DLP checks, and refusal/justification policies. Policies should be enforced out-of-band from the model (e.g., middleware) and produce auditable decisions.

Key practices: tag data with provenance (source, trust level, tenant) and preserve it through the pipeline; restrict capabilities based on provenance; use per-tenant memory/vector-store namespaces and scoped credentials; limit context sharing across sessions; add self-check or verifier models that critique actions against policy; and employ sandboxes/timeouts/quotas for any code execution. For RAG, treat retrieved text as data only: strip scripts, normalize, and strictly template prompts so that untrusted content cannot alter instructions.

• Role and context separation: Process untrusted content in compartments with no tool authority; pass only structured, minimal summaries forward.
• Independent policy layer: Middleware that validates inputs/outputs/tool calls (allowlists, argument checks, DLP/PII rules) regardless of prompt phrasing.
• Provenance and tenancy: Tag data with source/tenant and enforce per-tenant isolation for memories, indices, and credentials.

• Separate untrusted content from authority: compartmentalize roles and never grant tools to channels that ingest untrusted text.
• Enforce an independent policy layer to validate and gate actions, inputs, and outputs.
• Preserve provenance and tenant boundaries across memory, indices, and credentials.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand how to isolate prompts and enforce policies that make LLM applications resilient to prompt injection.

body.en:
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems pull content from a knowledge store and pass it to an LLM as context. Attackers exploit this by poisoning data sources (e.g., uploading or modifying documents) to insert prompt-injection instructions, deceptive links, or misleading facts that the model may follow or repeat.

Poisoning can occur at ingestion (malicious files, altered metadata), indexing (manipulating chunking/keywords to dominate retrieval), or at query time (serving updated content through remote references). Effective defenses combine provenance and integrity controls for data, aggressive sanitization and isolation of retrieved text, retrieval/ranking safeguards, and continuous monitoring and red teaming to measure and reduce attack success rate.

• RAG poisoning: Inserting or modifying content so the retriever surfaces adversarial text that steers model behavior or facts.
• Prompt injection via context: Malicious instructions embedded in retrieved passages that try to override system or developer prompts.
• Data supply chain security: Provenance, signing, access control, and review processes that protect ingestion, storage, and indexing.

• RAG poisoning targets ingestion, indexing, and retrieval to surface adversarial content.
• Treat retrieved text as untrusted: sanitize, compartmentalize, and prevent it from acting as instructions.
• Secure the data supply chain with provenance, integrity checks, access control, monitoring, and routine red-team exercises.
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You can now recognize how malicious documents poison RAG systems and apply layered defenses across ingestion, retrieval, and prompt handling.

In this lesson you will learn: 1) Common weaknesses in embeddings and vector search exploited to skew retrieval 2) Risks including norm exploitation, hubness, collisions, and vector-store poisoning 3) Defensive configurations, monitoring, and governance to harden embedding pipelines

Embeddings map text to vectors so similarity search can retrieve relevant passages. Weaknesses arise from distance metrics, high-dimensional effects, and index approximations that adversaries can game.

For example, if dot-product is used without normalization, high-norm vectors can dominate rankings, and hubness can cause a few vectors to appear similar to many queries. Attackers can insert crafted vectors or documents to hijack results, or exploit shared indexes to leak information.

Robust defenses include normalization and metric selection, hybrid retrieval with reranking, per-tenant isolation, provenance for vectors, monitoring for outliers/hubs, and versioned, tested embedding models.

**In this lesson you will learn:**

- 1) How sensitive data leaks occur in LLM and RAG systems (prompts, retrieved docs, tools, logs, training data)
- 2) Prevention and detection techniques including retrieval scoping, PII/secret redaction, DLP, and egress controls
- 3) How to test and red-team for disclosure risks using realistic attack scenarios and monitoring.

Sensitive data disclosure arises when an LLM reveals PII, PHI, secrets, or confidential business data via inputs, retrieved documents, tools, memory, or logs. In RAG, prompt-injected or untrusted content can steer the model to exfiltrate data or bypass instructions; retrieval must be constrained by authorization, not just similarity.

Models may regurgitate rare strings memorized during training, and attackers can attempt membership or extraction attacks, so minimize exposure and avoid feeding secrets. Apply least-privilege retrieval with document- and tenant-level ACLs, attribute-based access control, and per-request filtering on metadata.

Redact or tokenize PII and secrets at ingestion; use DLP/secret scanners and context-aware policies on both inputs and outputs. Protect logs and telemetry with client-side redaction, encryption, short retention, and strict access controls.

Enforce egress allowlists for tools and connectors, and add runtime guards (policy checks, classifiers) with fail-closed behavior and clear user-safe fallbacks. Continuously test with adversarial prompts, canary data, and attack simulations to validate controls.

• Data leakage vectors: Prompt injection, over-broad retrieval, tool/connector misuse, model regurgitation, and logging/analytics exposure
• Retrieval scoping: Document- and tenant-aware filters (ABAC), metadata guards, deny/allow lists, and per-request auth enforced before generation
• Input/output protection: PII/secret redaction, DLP and pattern/ML classifiers, canary tokens, egress controls, and privacy-preserving logging

• Enforce least-privilege retrieval with tenant/document ACLs and metadata filters
• Apply input/output DLP, secret scanning, and egress allowlists with fail-closed policies
• Red-team with prompt injection, canaries, and monitoring to continuously validate controls
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You now understand how sensitive data disclosure happens in LLM/RAG systems and how to prevent, detect, and respond to it in practice.

title.en: Dependencies, models and dataset supply chain

body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) How supply-chain risks affect libraries, models, datasets, tools, and connectors 2) How to verify provenance and integrity using signing, attestations, and reproducible builds 3) How to operationalize pinning, scanning, isolation, and safe rollout/rollback for updates.

LLM application supply chains span packages, containers, models/weights, datasets, prompt templates, and third-party APIs. Threats include typosquatting, compromised maintainers, dependency confusion, weight tampering/backdoors, and dataset poisoning.

Mitigate by pinning versions with hashes, using lockfiles and private/allowlisted registries, verifying checksums and signatures (e.g., Sigstore), and capturing build/test attestations (e.g., in-toto/SLSA). Maintain SBOMs and model/dataset “bills of materials,” track licenses, and document provenance via model cards and datasheets.

Sanitize and curate datasets (PII scrubbing, deduplication), and detect poisoning with outlier detection, trigger/activation tests, and canary evaluations. Isolate training/inference with minimal base images, content-addressed storage, and egress allowlists; secure secrets with a KMS and rotate keys.

Before adoption or updates, quarantine and evaluate artifacts, run automated security/eval tests, and use canary releases with fast rollback and monitoring.

• Provenance and attestation: Signed artifacts, checksums, SBOMs/attestations (e.g., SLSA) to confirm who built what, how, and when
• Dependency management: Private indices/allowlists, version and hash pinning, vulnerability scanning, and reproducible builds
• Dataset/model integrity: Poisoning/backdoor detection, curation and PII scrubbing, evaluation gates, and secure storage/access

• Treat models, datasets, and tools as supply-chain artifacts: pin, sign, attest, and scan them
• Isolate build/inference, restrict egress, and protect secrets; test updates behind canaries with fast rollback
• Curate and monitor datasets to prevent poisoning and backdoors; maintain SBOMs and provenance records
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You can now evaluate and secure the dependencies, models, and datasets in your LLM/RAG supply chain.

title.en: Excessive Agency and Least Privilege in LLM Agents

body.en:
Excessive agency occurs when an LLM agent is granted more permissions, capabilities, or autonomy than it needs to fulfill its intended function. This creates a significantly enlarged attack surface: a compromised or manipulated agent can read sensitive files, call destructive APIs, exfiltrate data, or pivot to other systems.

The least privilege principle—borrowed from classical system security—states that every component should operate with only the minimum permissions required. Applied to LLM agents, this means scoping file-system access, restricting which APIs can be called, limiting database operations to read-only where writes are unnecessary, and ensuring the agent cannot spawn sub-processes or create persistent side-effects without explicit authorization.

Real-world incidents have shown agents deleting production records, sending unauthorized emails, and triggering financial transactions because developers granted broad permissions for convenience. Mapping each agent action to a business justification and enforcing permission boundaries at the infrastructure layer—not just in the prompt—is essential defensive practice.

title.en: Tool Allowlists, Scopes, Approvals, and Sandboxes

body.en:
A tool allowlist enumerates every tool or function an agent is permitted to invoke. Any tool not on the list is categorically unavailable, preventing adversaries from tricking the agent into using dangerous capabilities via prompt injection.

Scopes refine the allowlist further: even an allowed tool—such as a file-system reader—can be scoped to specific directories, preventing lateral access. OAuth scopes, database roles, and API key restrictions are common implementation vehicles.

Approval workflows introduce a human checkpoint before the agent executes high-risk, irreversible, or high-cost actions such as deleting records, sending communications, or initiating payments. Well-designed approvals present the human with a clear summary of the proposed action and its consequences.

Sandboxes isolate agent execution at the OS, container, or VM level. Code execution sandboxes like gVisor, Firecracker, or cloud-based ephemeral environments ensure that even if an agent is fully compromised, its ability to interact with the broader infrastructure is physically constrained by the sandbox boundary.

body.en:
A tool allowlist enumerates every tool or function an agent is permitted to invoke. Any tool not on the list is categorically unavailable, preventing adversaries from tricking the agent into using dangerous capabilities via prompt injection.

Scopes refine the allowlist further: even an allowed tool—such as a file-system reader—can be scoped to specific directories, preventing lateral access. OAuth scopes, database roles, and API key restrictions are common implementation vehicles.

Approval workflows introduce a human checkpoint before the agent executes high-risk, irreversible, or high-cost actions such as deleting records, sending communications, or initiating payments. Well-designed approvals present the human with a clear summary of the proposed action and its consequences.

Sandboxes isolate agent execution at the OS, container, or VM level. Code execution sandboxes like gVisor, Firecracker, or cloud-based ephemeral environments ensure that even if an agent is fully compromised, its ability to interact with the broader infrastructure is physically constrained by the sandbox boundary.

• **Tool Allowlist**: An explicit, enumerated list of tools an agent may call; all tools absent from the list are blocked by default.
• **Scope Restriction**: Limiting the operational domain of an allowed tool, e.g., read-only access to a specific S3 prefix rather than an entire bucket.
• **Human-in-the-Loop Approval**: A mandatory human review gate before execution of high-risk, costly, or irreversible agent actions.
• **Sandboxing**: Technical isolation of agent execution (container, VM, or microVM) to prevent breakout into the broader infrastructure regardless of what the agent does inside.

question.en: What is the primary security benefit of a tool allowlist for LLM agents?

text.en: It speeds up agent response times by preloading tool schemas
It prevents agents from invoking any tool not explicitly permitted, even under adversarial prompting
It logs all tool invocations for compliance purposes
It automatically updates tool permissions based on usage patterns

explanation.en: A tool allowlist enforces a default-deny policy on tool invocations, ensuring that prompt injection or adversarial manipulation cannot trick the agent into calling unauthorized tools.

question.en: An LLM agent is permitted to use a code execution tool. Which additional control best limits the damage if the agent is manipulated into running malicious code?

text.en: Adding a warning in the system prompt to avoid running dangerous code
Running the code execution tool inside an isolated sandbox environment
Restricting the agent to Python only, disabling other languages
Requiring the agent to explain the code before executing it

explanation.en: A sandbox provides hard technical isolation. Even if the agent executes malicious code, the sandbox boundary prevents that code from reaching the host system or broader infrastructure.

question.en: For which type of agent action is a human-in-the-loop approval workflow most critically needed?

text.en: Fetching a webpage to summarize its content
Looking up a product's current price in a database
Initiating a wire transfer on behalf of a user
Converting a temperature from Celsius to Fahrenheit

explanation.en: Human-in-the-loop approvals are most critical for irreversible, high-impact actions such as financial transactions. Read-only or trivially reversible operations present much lower risk.

title.en: Unbounded Consumption and Cost Abuse in LLM Systems

body.en:
Unbounded consumption refers to scenarios where an LLM application uses computational resources, API calls, or tokens without enforced limits. This can arise from legitimate bugs—such as infinite agentic loops—or from deliberate adversarial exploitation.

Attack vectors include prompt injections that instruct an agent to recursively call itself, crafted inputs that maximize token usage in responses, and abuse of public-facing endpoints to exhaust an organization's API quota or billing credits. In multi-agent architectures, a single malicious instruction can cascade across dozens of sub-agents, each consuming tokens and making downstream API calls.

Defenses operate at multiple layers: per-user and per-session token budgets enforced at the gateway level, maximum iteration limits on agentic loops, circuit breakers that halt execution when cost thresholds are exceeded, and real-time cost monitoring with automated alerts. Input length limits and output truncation policies further reduce the token surface available to attackers. Organizations should also implement billing anomaly detection and maintain hard spending limits at the cloud provider level to provide a final backstop.

question.en: Which attack pattern most directly exploits the unbounded consumption vulnerability in an agentic LLM system?

text.en: Injecting SQL into a database query tool
A prompt injection that causes the agent to enter an infinite recursive loop of API calls
Extracting the system prompt through carefully crafted user messages
Bypassing authentication by manipulating session tokens

explanation.en: A prompt injection triggering an infinite recursive loop directly exploits unbounded consumption by causing the agent to make unlimited API calls, exhausting token budgets and incurring runaway costs.

question.en: What is the role of a circuit breaker in defending against unbounded consumption?

text.en: It encrypts all API calls to prevent eavesdropping
It automatically halts agent execution when a predefined cost or iteration limit is reached
It routes traffic to a backup LLM provider when the primary is unavailable
It validates all tool inputs against a schema before execution

explanation.en: A circuit breaker monitors consumption metrics and stops the process automatically when defined thresholds are exceeded, preventing runaway resource usage from completing unchecked.

question.en: Which of the following represents the most comprehensive defense-in-depth approach against cost abuse?

text.en: Relying on the LLM provider's built-in abuse detection alone
Asking users to agree to a terms-of-service clause prohibiting abuse
Combining per-session token budgets, iteration limits, real-time monitoring, and hard cloud-level spending caps
Limiting the application to a single agent with no tool access

explanation.en: Defense-in-depth requires multiple independent controls. Combining gateway-level budgets, loop iteration limits, real-time alerting, and cloud billing caps ensures that failure of any single control does not result in catastrophic cost abuse.

title.en: Security Regression Tests and Report Writing for LLM Systems

body.en:
Security regression tests ensure that vulnerabilities discovered during red-team exercises do not silently reappear as the system evolves. For LLM agent applications, a regression suite should include prompt injection payloads that previously succeeded, tool invocation attempts that should be blocked, cost-abuse scenarios with input crafted to maximize token usage, and access-control probes targeting over-permissioned paths. These tests must be automated and integrated into the CI/CD pipeline so that every deployment is validated against the known threat catalog.

A professional red-team report for an AI system follows a structured format: an executive summary for leadership, a technical narrative describing the assessment methodology and scope, individual finding sections with reproducible steps and evidence, a severity rating using a standard scale such as CVSS or a custom AI-risk rubric, and a prioritized remediation roadmap. Each finding must clearly state the attack scenario, the business impact, and a concrete mitigation with implementation guidance.

Effective report writing bridges the gap between security research and engineering action. Ambiguous findings stall remediation; precise, reproducible write-ups accelerate it. Including regression test cases derived from each finding creates a direct feedback loop between reporting and ongoing assurance.

question.en: What is the primary purpose of including security regression tests in a CI/CD pipeline for an LLM application?

text.en: To measure the latency of agent tool invocations under load
To ensure previously discovered vulnerabilities are automatically detected if they reappear in future deployments
To validate that the LLM produces grammatically correct outputs
To benchmark the model's accuracy on domain-specific tasks

explanation.en: Security regression tests embedded in CI/CD pipelines catch vulnerability regressions automatically, preventing known issues from silently resurfacing as the codebase evolves.

question.en: Which section of a red-team report is most important for a non-technical executive audience?

text.en: The detailed technical reproduction steps for each finding
The raw network traffic logs captured during testing
The executive summary, which communicates overall risk posture and business impact
The appendix containing all prompt injection payloads used

explanation.en: The executive summary translates technical findings into business risk language. It is the section leadership relies on to understand the overall risk posture and to make prioritization and investment decisions.

question.en: What makes a red-team finding 'actionable' in a professional report?

text.en: It includes the exact number of tokens consumed during the attack
It describes the vulnerability in academic theoretical terms without operational detail
It provides reproducible steps, a severity rating, business impact, and a concrete mitigation with implementation guidance
It lists all tools used by the red team regardless of relevance to the finding

explanation.en: An actionable finding gives engineering teams everything they need: how to reproduce the issue, how severe it is, why it matters to the business, and exactly how to fix it. Without all four elements, remediation is delayed or incomplete.
